title: Last Day Where You Can Still Cross
statement:
A grid has `row` rows and `col` columns, numbered from 1, and on day 0 every cell is dry land. On day `d` (for `d = 1, 2, ...`), the cell `cells[d - 1] = [r, c]` (row `r`, column `c`, both 1-based) turns into water and stays water for good.

On a given day you can cross if some walk exists that starts on any land cell of the first row, finishes on any land cell of the last row, visits only land cells, and steps only up, down, left or right. Return the largest day number on which crossing is still possible.
constraints: All pairs in cells are distinct
signature: int latestDayToCross(int row, int col, int[][] cells)
notes:
## Intuition

Water only ever spreads, so once crossing fails it fails forever: the days on which you can cross form a prefix `0, 1, ..., answer`. That monotone yes/no shape is exactly what binary search on the answer needs. For one candidate day, flood the first `day` cells and run a breadth-first search from the dry top row; crossing works if it touches the last row. Re-checking every day one by one would cost O((row·col)²); binary search needs only about log(row·col) checks.

## Approach

1. Write `canCross(day)`: mark the first `day` cells as `blocked`, push every dry top-row cell into `queue` (blocking it so it is visited once), and run BFS in the four `directions`.
2. As soon as a dequeued cell is in the last row, return `true`; if the queue drains, return `false`.
3. Binary search with `left = 0` (day 0 is all land, so it always works) and `right = cells.length`.
4. Take the upper middle `mid`. If `canCross(mid)`, the answer is at least `mid`, so `left = mid`; otherwise it is below, so `right = mid - 1`.
5. When they meet, `left` is the last good day.

## Example 1, step by step

`row = col = 2`, `cells = [[1,1],[2,1],[1,2],[2,2]]`. Start `left = 0`, `right = 4`. `mid = 2`: cells (1,1) and (2,1) are water, but column 2 is dry, so crossing works and `left = 2`. `mid = 3`: (1,2) is also water, the top row is gone, so `right = 2`. The loop ends and returns `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(row·col·log(row·col)): each check builds the grid and runs BFS in O(row·col).
- Space: O(row·col) for `blocked` and the queue.

## Pitfalls

- `cells` is 1-based; subtract 1 from both coordinates.
- With `left = mid`, `mid` must round up, or the loop never ends when `right = left + 1`.
- Mark a cell as `blocked` when it is pushed, not when it is popped, or cells get queued many times.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `blocked` | water cells plus cells the BFS already queued |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue and the index of the next cell to process |
| `r`, `c` / `nr`, `nc` | current cell / its neighbour (0-based) |
| `left`, `right` | range that still contains the answer |
| `mid` | candidate day being tested |
